Moshe Lazar, son of Rachel and Yaakov, was born in the town of Mezritch, Poland (then part of Russia). He studied in a *heder* and from 1916 in a reformed Talmud Torah. In 1924 the family immigrated to the Land of Israel. His devout parents had agreed to the request of his grandmother, who lived in Jerusalem and asked that they look after their only son and raise him as a Jew who walks in the ways of his forefathers. Moshe-Yitzchak was accepted to a yeshiva in Jerusalem and continued his studies there. As he grew older, however, he drifted away from his family's tradition and chose to follow the path of the new Yishuv. He learned the printing trade and for several years earned a living as a hand compositor in a printing house. His next step was joining the Haganah, the pre-state Jewish defense organization, where he held responsible positions and was later counted among the command staff of the Jerusalem district. During the 1929 riots he was among the defenders of the Old City. When his parents heard of this, they hurried to the Land of Israel to bring him back to the right path. But upon arriving they realized that their paths had parted completely, and they left the country as sorrowful as they had come. In the meantime, longing grew on both sides, and eventually his parents returned to the country a second time and reconciled with him. He, who worked as a driver in Jerusalem, also took care of their livelihood.

As the situation in the city worsened and the War of Independence broke out following the UN General Assembly's partition resolution, Moshe was drafted into the Etzioni Brigade. The road to Mount Scopus passed through the Arab neighborhood of Sheikh Jarrah, and once the war began, movement to the mountain was possible only in convoys protected by the British army. On the morning of 13 April 1948, a convoy set out for Mount Scopus after the British had assured that the road was open and safe. The convoy was ambushed in Sheikh Jarrah, and hundreds of Arabs poured heavy fire on it. Some of the vehicles managed to extricate themselves and return, but two buses, an ambulance, and an escort armored vehicle were trapped in the ambush. For many hours the convoy's men fought and tried to prevent the Arabs from approaching the vehicles. Fire from our positions in the city and on Mount Scopus, as well as armored vehicles sent to the scene, could not help the convoy. British army forces present at the site did not intervene and did nothing to assist, despite appeals to them. In the afternoon the Arabs succeeded in setting both buses on fire with their passengers inside. Only toward evening did the British intervene and rescue the survivors from the trapped vehicles. Moshe was among those who fell on Wednesday, 4 Nisan 5708 (13 April 1948). He was laid to rest in the Sanhedria cemetery in Jerusalem.
